title: India’s IT Stocks Have Lost 27 Per Cent This Year. For NRI Tech Workers, the Pain Is Doubly Personal.
excerpt: The Nifty IT index has shed more than a quarter of its value in 2026 as AI disruption fears collide with macro headwinds. For the millions of Indian-origin professionals who work in the same industry they invest in, the exposure is uniquely concentrated.
body:
The Nifty IT index has fallen 27 per cent in 2026. In just seven consecutive trading sessions through June 12, it shed 11.5 per cent. TCS, Infosys, Wipro, and HCL Tech have all hit fresh 52-week lows. The sector that once made India a stock market heavyweight has become its heaviest drag.

For NRI technology professionals — the software engineers, product managers, data scientists, and architects who form the backbone of the Indian diaspora’s professional class — this is not an abstract portfolio event. It is a collision of career risk and investment risk that few other communities face with the same intensity.

What Triggered the Rout

Three forces converged to create the worst stretch for Indian IT stocks in recent memory.

The first is AI disruption. Generative AI tools have advanced to the point where investors now believe they will cause 2 to 3 per cent annual revenue deflation in traditional IT services over the coming years. The logic is straightforward: if AI can write, review, and maintain code at a fraction of the cost, the billable-hour model that underpins Indian IT outsourcing faces structural compression. When Anthropic launched its latest suite of AI tools in early June, the Nifty IT index fell another 1.6 per cent in a single session.

“The key concern is that productivity improvements in software engineering are occurring much faster than in non-software domains,” said Sumit Pokharna, senior vice president of fundamental research at Kotak Securities.

The second force is macroeconomic. U.S. consumer inflation accelerated to 4.2 per cent in May, its fastest pace in three years, raising the possibility that the Federal Reserve could maintain its hawkish stance or even consider additional rate hikes. Indian IT firms derive the bulk of their revenue from U.S. clients. Higher rates mean tighter corporate technology budgets, delayed digital transformation projects, and reduced discretionary spending on the consulting and managed services that generate India’s IT margins.

The third is the broader rotation out of India. Foreign investors have pulled a record $30 billion from Indian equities in 2026, redirecting capital to semiconductor-heavy markets like South Korea and Taiwan. India’s weight in the MSCI Emerging Markets Index has declined from 12.82 per cent in February to 10.87 per cent in May. The country’s stock market has slipped to seventh place globally by market capitalisation, overtaken by Taiwan and South Korea in the past month alone.

The Double Exposure Problem

The financial pain for NRI tech workers is amplified by a concentration risk that is almost unique to this community.

Many Indian-origin tech professionals hold ESOPs or RSUs in Indian IT companies — TCS, Infosys, and Wipro are among the largest employers of H-1B visa holders and global technology talent. Their equity compensation is denominated in the same sector that is under pressure.

Simultaneously, their retirement portfolios, mutual fund SIPs, and family investments in India are often disproportionately allocated to IT-sector funds and large-cap indices where IT stocks carry significant weight. The Nifty 50 itself has IT as one of its largest sector allocations.

And their careers depend on the same industry. If AI disruption reduces demand for traditional IT services, it is not just stock prices that fall — it is headcount, utilisation rates, and the annual increment cycles that have powered NRI wealth accumulation for two decades.

This triple exposure — equity compensation, portfolio allocation, and career income all tied to the same sector — is a concentration risk that financial advisers rarely address because it requires understanding both the Indian market structure and the specific employment patterns of the diaspora.

The Contrarian Case

Not everyone is bearish. Lighthouse Canton, a global wealth and asset management firm with more than $5 billion in assets, argued on June 12 that India’s lack of direct AI exposure could prove an “advantage of absence.”

Abhay Laijawala, the firm’s chief investment officer for India, told Reuters that when sector concentration in markets like South Korea and Taiwan reaches current levels, investors tend to fatally underprice the possibility that a risk could emerge from outside the core business model. Both markets have logged foreign outflows in June, suggesting investors have begun trimming exposure.

India, Laijawala argued, offers a deep listed universe tied to the next phase of AI spending — power infrastructure, data centres, electrical equipment, cooling systems, engineering, and capital goods. “We have plenty of picks and shovels,” he said.

BlackRock, the world’s largest asset manager, echoed the sentiment earlier in the week, calling India’s equity market “over-punished” for lacking a direct AI play. India remains one of the firm’s highest-conviction medium- to long-term emerging market positions, supported by demographics, infrastructure spending, and indirect AI-linked opportunities.

What NRI Investors Can Do

The immediate priority is to audit concentration. An NRI tech worker holding Infosys ESOPs, investing in a Nifty 50 index fund, and working at an IT services company has effectively made one very large bet on the same underlying variable.

Diversification does not require abandoning conviction in India. It means reallocating within Indian equities toward sectors less exposed to AI deflation risk — banking, defence, infrastructure, power, and consumer staples. It means considering the FCNR deposit opportunity that the RBI has just opened, where dollar deposits now yield up to 7 per cent with government-backed hedging. And it means separating career risk from portfolio risk by ensuring that at least a portion of investable assets sits in geographies and sectors uncorrelated with Indian IT services.

The Nifty IT index may recover. India’s IT sector has survived multiple existential narratives before — the Y2K cliff, the 2008 financial crisis, the automation scare of the mid-2010s. But this time, the disruption is coming from inside the house, from the very technology that Indian IT workers are building. That paradox deserves a more thoughtful response than hoping the chart turns green.
